name: Implicit Surface Primitives
text:
# Implicit Surface Primitives

## Overview
Implicit Surface Primitives represent 3D geometry as the zero-level set of a scalar field function $f(\mathbf{x})$, where the surface is the locus of points where $f(\mathbf{x}) = 0$ [G]. This family solves the problem of representing complex, smooth, or dynamic geometry without polygonal meshes, enabling operations like boolean blending, smooth deformation, and efficient ray marching [G]. It is distinguished from polygonal representations by its continuity and from procedural noise volumes by its focus on sharp or smoothly blended boundaries rather than volumetric density gradients [G].

## Shared principles
Builds on the parent family's core mechanism of domain definition, value assignment, and storage/access [13-procedural-and-implicit-volumes.md]. All methods in this family evaluate a scalar field $f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$ at a query point $\mathbf{x}$, where the sign of $f(\mathbf{x})$ typically indicates spatial position: negative for inside, positive for outside, and zero on the surface [G]. Key shared characteristics include analytic or procedural definition, local or global support, composition via set operations or blending, and point-wise evaluation optimized for GPU parallelism or ray marching step sizes [G].

## Subtopics

### [Metaball Field Evaluation](1017-metaball-field-evaluation.md)
[Metaball Field Evaluation](#1017-metaball-field-evaluation.md) is a procedural method for generating and updating a 3D scalar density volume representing dynamic metaballs (spheres) using compute or fragment shaders. It solves the problem of efficiently computing the scalar field values for a large number of moving volumetric primitives on the GPU, often serving as input for subsequent raycasting or marching cubes algorithms. It distinguishes itself from static implicit surface definitions by supporting real-time animation of blob positions and strengths, and from simple sphere blending by using an inverse-square distance falloff with a threshold offset rather than a smooth Gaussian blend. Choose it when real-time animation of blobby volumes is required.

### [Distance to Hypertextures](1555-distance-to-hypertextures.md)
[Distance to Hypertextures](#1555-distance-to-hypertextures.md) is a technique for adding geometric relief and detail to surfaces without increasing polygon count by evaluating procedural noise within a volumetric region around the object rather than solely on the surface. It deforms implicit surfaces by adding procedural noise to the function's range instead of the domain, enabling the use of sphere tracing with safe distance bounds. This method bridges the gap between surface textures and volumetric phenomena, allowing for the modeling of complex, organic details. Choose it when surface detail is needed without increasing polygon count.

### [Superelliptic Blends](2051-superelliptic-blends.md)
[Superelliptic blends](#2051-superelliptic-blends.md) (also known as pseudonorm blends) are a local blending technique for implicit surfaces that computes the $p$-norm distance to the blended union of signed distance functions (SDFs). Unlike global blending methods, this approach operates only within the overlapping support of the constituent functions, defined by the parameter $\epsilon$. It is distinguished by its computational simplicity and compatibility with sphere tracing, though it introduces gradient discontinuities at the boundary of the blend domain. Choose it when smooth, local blending of SDFs is required without global recomputation.

### [Implicit Field Composition](2652-implicit-field-composition.md)
[Implicit Field Composition](#2652-implicit-field-composition.md) constructs complex volumetric or surface geometries by combining primitive scalar fields (such as terrain, cuboids, and spheres) using set-theoretic operations like union and intersection. It differs from single-primitive methods by enabling the procedural generation of hybrid scenes, specifically serving as the signed distance field ([SDF](#1466-signed-distance-fields-sdf.md)) generator for dual contouring mesh extraction. Choose it when constructing complex scenes from multiple primitive types.

### [Soft Metablobby SDF](2753-soft-metablobby-sdf.md)
[Soft Metablobby SDF](#2753-soft-metablobby-sdf.md) defines a scalar field using piecewise cubic polynomials to approximate Gaussian blobby blending, avoiding expensive exponentiation and iterative root finding. It differs from standard Metaball Field Evaluation by using a localized, compact-support cubic kernel rather than a global Gaussian, providing smoother blends with lower computational cost per sample. Choose it when efficient, smooth blobby blending is needed without transcendental functions.

### [Implicit Surface Definition](2798-implicit-surface-definition.md)
[Implicit Surface Definition](#2798-implicit-surface-definition.md) provides the mathematical foundation for representing 3D geometry as the zero-level set of a scalar field $f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$. It solves the problem of defining complex shapes analytically without explicit mesh topology, allowing for smooth interpolation and Boolean operations. It differs from explicit surface definitions (like polygonal meshes) by defining volume occupancy via a continuous function rather than discrete vertices and faces, and from procedural volume data (like noise fields) by focusing on sharp or smoothly blended boundaries defined by isosurfaces. Choose it as the foundational reference for implicit surface mathematics.

### [Half-Space Field Generation](4006-half-space-field-generation.md)
[Half-Space Field Generation](#4006-half-space-field-generation.md) creates a binary scalar field that defines a simulation domain (typically a fluid) by partitioning space into "inside" and "outside" regions based on a threshold. It solves the problem of restricting physical simulation and rendering computations to a specific sub-volume, ignoring empty space or background media. Unlike smooth implicit primitives (e.g., SDFs or metaballs) that define continuous geometry, this method produces a discontinuous step function, effectively acting as a mask for the simulation grid. Choose it when simulating or rendering within a bounded half-space domain.

### [Implicit Geometry Sampling](6685-implicit-geometry-sampling.md)
[Implicit Geometry Sampling](#6685-implicit-geometry-sampling.md) is a technique for generating volume data from mathematical implicit functions, providing value and gradient at any point in space without discrete [voxel grids](#1719-voxel-grid-indexing.md). It enables on-the-fly evaluation of [implicit surfaces for rendering](#775-differentiable-volumetric-rendering-dvr.md) or simulation without precomputing a full voxel volume. Choose it when memory is constrained or when adaptive, continuous evaluation is preferred over discrete grids.

### [Specific Implicit Primitives](8499-specific-implicit-primitives.md)
Specific Implicit Primitives covers specialized implicit surface definitions for specific geometric shapes. These primitives provide optimized evaluation routines for standard forms like spheres, tori, and cylinders, often leveraging analytical distance formulas for faster ray marching compared to generic field compositions. Choose it when rendering standard geometric primitives with maximum performance.

### Compact Polynomial Kernel
A kernel family used to define skeleton-based implicit surfaces, characterized by local support required for efficient field evaluation on large skeletons and efficient closed-form evaluation of the integral field equation for line segment primitives with linearly interpolated prescribed thickness [S1]. The support of an individual primitive is a sphere-cone defined by scaling the two primitive endpoints' radius by a factor $\sigma$ [S1]. Parameters include the degree parameter $i$, which defines the polynomial degree of the kernel, and the scale parameter $\sigma$, which scales the primitive endpoints' radius to define the support of an individual primitive [S1]. Choose it when evaluating integral surfaces along skeletal structures with variable thickness.

## Background
Implicit surfaces were introduced by Wyvill et al. in the context of "blobby" objects for computer graphics [G]. The mathematical foundation relies on level set methods and signed distance functions (SDFs) [G]. The theoretical underpinnings of kernel-based implicit surfaces, including the Compact Polynomial, Cauchy, and Inverse kernels, are detailed in academic literature on integral surfaces [S1].
